title: The Trustworthy One
subtitle: Integrity, Character, and the Title of Al-Amin
summary: The youth of Muhammad ﷺ in Makkah, his preservation from pagan vices and idolatry, his modesty, his commercial integrity in partnership with al-Sa'ib, his reputation for truthfulness, his care for trusts, and how his people came to call him Al-Amin.

sections.text: The Social Environment of Pre-Islamic Makkah

As Muhammad ﷺ reached young adulthood in Makkah, the city around him was defined by deep tribal divisions, commercial ambition, and polytheistic ritualism. The sanctuary of the Kaaba, originally dedicated by the Prophet Ibrahim to the worship of the One God, had been surrounded by hundreds of stone idols and tribal deities, including Hubal, Isaf, and Na'ilah. Makkan society was driven by clan prestige, where personal worth was often measured by pedigree, wealth, and the capacity for aggressive tribal defense.

Yet amidst this environment, the biographers describe Muhammad as living apart from the common vices of his peers. He took no part in drinking gatherings, gambling with divining arrows, or the night revelries of the pre-Islamic era. A report transmitted by Ibn Ishaq and others, whose chain scholars have debated, relates that on the occasions he set out to join such gatherings in his youth, sleep overcame him and kept him away.

Furthermore, Muhammad observed the peace of the sacred months with scrupulous consistency. While factions within Arabia frequently engaged in opportunistic raids and violated sacred truces, his natural disposition was anchored in reverence for moral boundaries. He avoided the vulgar poetry, boasts of lineage, and tribal vanity that permeated the public squares of Makkah, establishing a reputation for dignified silence and thoughtful speech.
The quiet stone homes and mountain shadows surrounding the ancient city of Makkah.
Innate Aversion to Idolatrous Rituals

While the chiefs and common people of Quraysh brought sacrifices to stone altars and swore by al-Lat and al-'Uzza, the biographers report that Muhammad kept away from idol worship and did not take part in its rites. In Ibn Ishaq's account of the monk Bahira, when he was asked to swear by al-Lat and al-'Uzza, he replied that nothing was more hateful to him than they were.

This uprightness was joined to a deep modesty (haya'). His Companion Abu Sa'id al-Khudri described it in words preserved in Sahih al-Bukhari, adding that when he disliked something it could be seen in his face. An incident from his youth that shows the same modesty took place during the rebuilding of the Ka'bah, which is described later in this collection.
"The Prophet ﷺ was more modest than a virgin in her seclusion, and when he disliked something, it could be recognized in his face." — Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 3562
Commercial Dealings and Mutual Partnerships

As a young adult, Muhammad took part in the trade of the city. In a market where short measure, broken contracts and usury often caused disputes, the reports that survive of his dealings describe honesty, fulfilment of agreements and a refusal to wrangle with a partner.

A notable testimony to this character comes from al-Sa'ib ibn Abi al-Sa'ib, who had been Muhammad's business partner before Islam. When he later came to the Prophet as a Muslim and people began praising him, the Prophet said that he knew him best, and al-Sa'ib replied: 'You were my partner, and you were the best of partners; you never evaded me and never disputed with me.' The report shows that his honesty in trade was known long before his prophethood.

"You were my partner in the pre-Islamic era, and you were the best of partners; you never evaded me and never disputed with me." — Sunan Ibn Majah, Hadith 2287; with similar wording in Sunan Abi Dawud, Hadith 4836
Bustling merchant stalls in the ancient market squares of the Hijaz.
The Title Bestowed: Al-Sadiq and Al-Amin

Over the years, the people of Makkah came to recognize Muhammad's integrity in every area of life. Those setting out on long journeys would leave their valuables in his keeping, knowing they were safe with him. His people came to call him Al-Sadiq (The Truthful) and Al-Amin (The Trustworthy).

Ibn Ishaq, the early biographer of the Prophet, summarized Muhammad's standing during this period: 'He grew up, and Allah protected him from the indecencies of the pre-Islamic era, desiring his honor, until he became the most noble of his people in character, the finest in neighborliness, the greatest in forbearance, the most truthful in speech, and the most reliable in fulfilling trusts, so that his folk called him by no name other than Al-Amin.'

This reputation for keeping trusts (amanah) outlasted later hostility. Ibn Ishaq relates that even after he proclaimed Islam and faced bitter opposition from Quraysh, people in Makkah continued to leave their valuables with him, and that when he migrated to Madinah he instructed his cousin 'Ali to remain behind in Makkah for three days to return every trust to its owner.

This universal reputation for veracity formed an undeniable historical foundation. When the divine message was proclaimed decades later, even his fiercest tribal opponents could not accuse him of having ever uttered a lie. As recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, when Byzantine Emperor Heraclius later interrogated Abu Sufyan—then a leading opponent of Islam—about Muhammad's background, he asked: 'Did you ever accuse him of lying before he claimed what he claimed?' Abu Sufyan was compelled to answer honestly: 'No.' Heraclius remarked that a man who does not lie to his fellow humans will never fabricate a lie against God.

Through his exemplary character, devotion to family ties, and refusal to participate in injustice, Muhammad earned the enduring trust of all clans within Makkah. He stood as a pillar of dependability in a turbulent society, living a life of quiet dignity that prepared him for the monumental responsibilities of divine revelation.
